findings.claim: For the exam, the Eduqas analysis uses B major for the verses and A major for the choruses. Also in L2 exam_tip_html and twice in L3 content_html.
findings.truth: The board is never named in student-facing text on this platform. The key scheme itself is right: intro and verses in B major, chorus in A major.
findings.evidence: house rule (CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md banned strings); key scheme confirmed against a published section-by-section analysis (Hooktheory: verse B major, chorus A major, 93 BPM)

findings.claim: The instrumental sonorities include xylophones and marimbas... The instrumental sounds - including xylophones and marimbas - imitate the pitched percussion instruments found across the African continent. Repeated in the L3 mark scheme for question 6.
findings.truth: No xylophone or marimba is played on the record. The kalimba/marimba riff is synthesised on a Yamaha GS-1 and layered from several takes. The sounds imitate African pitched percussion.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Africa (Toto song): the kalimba riff was programmed on a Yamaha GS-1 and recorded six times with different rhythms, then layered; spec AoS4 examines how instrumental and synthesised sound is used

findings.claim: the chord revision sheet labels the intro chords in A major context as ♭VII, vi and ii
findings.truth: A, G#m and C#m are ♭VII, vi and ii of B MAJOR. In an A major reading the same chords would be I, vii and iii - which is exactly what the lesson's own mnemonic box says two paragraphs later.
findings.evidence: recomputation of the Roman numerals; the lesson's own mnemonic box states A (I/♭VII), G#m (vii/vi), C#m (iii/ii)

findings.claim: the 4-bar intro section is repeated four times (giving 8 bars percussion + 16 bars of Riff a/b = 24 bars total). L3 structure timeline repeats it as 'Played 4 times'.
findings.truth: Three statements, not four: 8 bars of percussion + 12 bars = 20 bars. A score bar lasts about 1.29 s (measured from four section boundaries that all land within 0.5 s), so 24 bars would run about 31 s, but Verse 1 verifiably enters at 0:24. L2 already says the intro plays the riff three times.
findings.evidence: verified timings (verse 1 0:24, chorus phrase 3 at 1:20, verse 2 1:43, instrumental 2:50, vocals return 3:05) reconciled against the lesson's own bar numbering; Hooktheory 93 BPM

findings.truth: E is a major triad on the fourth degree of B major, so the numeral is upper-case IV. Lower case iv would mean E minor. The neighbouring numerals in the same list (Ic, ♭VIIc) use the same figured-bass convention correctly.
findings.evidence: recomputation against the B major key signature given in the same lesson

findings.claim: Five question labels disagree with their own mark schemes: L1 q2 (label 1 mark, scheme 2), L1 q3 (label 4, scheme 3), L1 q6 (label 10, band ladder caps at 8), L3 q2 (label 4, scheme 'Max 2'), L3 q3 (label 4, scheme 'Max 3').
findings.truth: The label must state the marks the scheme actually awards, or students mis-time their answers.
findings.evidence: recomputation of each mark scheme; label vocabulary from scripts/pipeline_api_guides.py type_slugs

findings.claim: Quality of written communication will be assessed in this question (L1 q6 stem); QWC: Accurate use of musical terminology and clear, structured writing (L2 q6 scheme).
findings.truth: This qualification has no separate marks for quality of written communication. The appraising paper carries AO3 and AO4 only.
findings.evidence: spec: appraising paper, 1 hour 15 minutes, 96 marks, 40%, eight questions (two per area of study, six on unprepared extracts and two on set extracts); Africa: Toto (released 1982) is the AoS4 prepared extract; AO3 20% + AO4 20% only

findings.claim: Two cards are mangled cloze deletions: one answers 'Background' from a section heading, the other answers 'David' from the songwriters' names.
findings.truth: Neither card is answerable. Single-word answers need a question that starts What/Which/Who/When/Name. Replaced with 'Which album was Africa recorded for?' (Toto IV) and 'Who wrote Africa?' (David Paich and Jeff Porcaro).
findings.evidence: flashcard rules; Wikipedia, Africa (Toto song): recorded June 1981 for Toto IV, written by David Paich and Jeff Porcaro

findings.claim: vi - IV - I - V (1 mark) OR F#m - D - A - E (1 mark). ... 1 marks for each correct chord in sequence if given individually, up to 4 marks.
findings.truth: The scheme awards 1 mark for the whole progression and 4 marks for the same four chords listed one at a time. Rewritten as 1 mark per correct chord in the right order, up to 4.
findings.evidence: recomputation; the question is labelled 4 marks

findings.claim: Extended-response questions (10 or 12 marks) expect you to discuss several musical elements
findings.truth: The paper sets ONE question that requires a longer response, and the spec gives no mark total for it. The plural and the mark figures are not supported.
findings.evidence: spec: appraising paper, 1 hour 15 minutes, 96 marks, 40%, eight questions (two per area of study, six on unprepared extracts and two on set extracts); Africa: Toto (released 1982) is the AoS4 prepared extract; AO3 20% + AO4 20% only; 'there will be one question which requires learners to write a longer response to a piece of music'

findings.claim: When the exam says “you will hear the music four times,” use each listening to focus on different elements.
findings.truth: The spec nowhere fixes the number of playings; the paper states it per question. The revision strategy is kept but no longer promises four playings.
findings.evidence: spec: appraising paper, 1 hour 15 minutes, 96 marks, 40%, eight questions (two per area of study, six on unprepared extracts and two on set extracts); Africa: Toto (released 1982) is the AoS4 prepared extract; AO3 20% + AO4 20% only; no statement anywhere in the spec on the number of playings

findings.claim: All three lessons reproduce complete lines of the song's words - four lines in the L1 verse timeline, seven across the L2 chorus and verse timelines, and further lines in L3 content, conclusion and two mark schemes.
findings.truth: This is an in-copyright 1982 song reproduced without a licence on a commercial site. Sections should be named and timed (for example 'Verse 1, phrase 2, bars 14-22') rather than quoted. The rewrite is too large to be surgical, so it is not in _edits.json.
findings.evidence: copyright distancing house rule; the song is in copyright and the platform is commercial

findings.claim: L1 lists the form as Intro, Verse 1, Chorus 1, Link 1, Verse 2, Chorus 2, Link 2, Instrumental, Chorus 3, Chorus 4, Outro.
findings.truth: L3's full structure walkthrough has no Chorus 4 - it runs Instrumental, Chorus 3, Outro. One of the two is wrong. The recording leaves room for either reading (the fade starts at about 4:00), so the score decides it. Recommend deleting Chorus 4 from the L1 list to match L3, unless the score shows a separate final chorus.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction between L1 and L3; verified timings (instrumental 2:50, fade from about 4:00) fit both readings

findings.claim: Chorus 3 covers bars 40–92 of the score and is 22 bars long.
findings.truth: Bars 40 to 92 is 53 bars, not 22. The figures can only be reconciled if the score jumps (for example bars 40-51 then 83-92, which is 22 bars). The bar range or the length needs correcting against the printed score, which I do not have.
findings.evidence: arithmetic; the unit's own bar map (intro 1-4, verse 5-39, chorus 40-57, link 58-65, instrumental 66-82, outro 93-96) leaves only bars 83-92 unaccounted for

findings.claim: L1 defines Riff a as bars 1-2 (2 bars). L2 says the 8-bar link is 'Riff a played twice' with a 4-bar chord pattern each time, and L3 agrees.
findings.truth: Riff a is 2 bars in L1 and 4 bars in L2 and L3. The 4-bar unit is really Riff a plus Riff b. Students will get the bar counts wrong. Recommend making L2 and L3 say 'the 4-bar intro pattern (Riff a and Riff b)'.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction; the chord content quoted in L2 (A - G#m - C#m - C#m) is exactly L1's Riff a plus Riff b

findings.claim: The Chorus 1 entry in the L3 structure timeline is labelled with two vocal incipits, the first of which belongs to Verse 1's fourth phrase and to the instrumental's vocal return, not to the chorus.
findings.truth: L1 and L2 both place that line in Verse 1 phrase 4 (bars 32-39) and at bars 78-82. Only the second incipit is chorus material. The fix sits inside the lyric rewrite of F12, so it is not in _edits.json.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction between L1, L2 and L3

findings.claim: Africa was released as the third single from the album on 30th September 1982 through Columbia Records.
findings.truth: The date is contested. Wikipedia gives 25 June 1982 (UK) and 7 October 1982 (US), and calls it the second single in Europe and the third in the US. Not corrected because no single true value could be established.

findings.claim: The flattened seventh chord is written ♭VII in L1 content but ♮VII in the L1 questions and throughout L2 and L3.
findings.truth: Both notations are defensible, but one should be used across the unit. Not corrected because it is presentational, not factual.

summary: 18 findings across all three lessons, 27 edits. The bar map (intro 1-4, verse 5-39, chorus 40-57, link 58-65, instrumental 66-82) was validated against the verified recording timings to within 0.5 s, which confirms the 2/2 barring and the B major / A major key scheme but rules out the four-times intro repeat. The unresolved items are the unlicensed song lyrics, the Chorus 3 bar range, the Chorus 4 entry and the two different lengths given for Riff a.
